explanations.answer: To test him with hard questions
explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. The queen of Sheba heard about Solomon's fame concerning the name of the LORD, and she came "…to test him with difficult questions." (1 Kings 10:1) Solomon, king of Israel, was the one answering. She packed a whole caravan just to quiz one man, and most people won't even drive to the store for a missing cup of flour.

Good guess, baker, but soldiers never come up. The text says she came "…to test him with difficult questions." (1 Kings 10:1) The queen of Sheba came with her questions and her curiosity. Nobody in this passage is recruiting an army.

explanations.answer: To end a war between them
explanations.explanation: I see why you'd think that, baker, because a queen showing up with a caravan sounds serious. But the text mentions no war at all. She heard about Solomon's fame and came "…to test him with difficult questions." (1 Kings 10:1) Her caravan was hauling spices, gold and precious stones, and that reads more like a visit than a peace treaty to me.

Gold it is, baker. The text says her caravan came "…with camels bearing spices, gold in great abundance, and precious stones." (1 Kings 10:2) That's a lot of weight for a camel to carry. I think those camels were ready for a nap by the time they got to Jerusalem.

Close, baker, since silver shows up later in this passage. But for her caravan, the text says "…gold in great abundance…" (1 Kings 10:2) Silver comes up in Solomon's own story, where it's accounted as nothing in his days (1 Kings 10:21). Her camels were loaded with spices, gold and precious stones.

Ivory does appear in this passage, baker, just not on her camels. Her caravan carried "…spices, gold in great abundance, and precious stones." (1 Kings 10:2) The ivory belongs to Solomon's great throne and to the cargo of the ships of Tarshish (1 Kings 10:18, 22). Easy to mix up when this much treasure is flying around.

Not quite, baker. The text says the opposite: "…Solomon answered all her questions; nothing was too difficult for the king to explain." (1 Kings 10:3) She came to test him, and every question got an answer. I'd have been sweating through my apron by question two.

That's right, baker. "…Solomon answered all her questions; nothing was too difficult for the king to explain." (1 Kings 10:3) She brought difficult questions, and he had an answer for every one. Think of someone going through their whole list and never getting stuck once.

You got it, baker. After she saw Solomon's wisdom, his palace, his table and his attendants, the text says "…it took her breath away." (1 Kings 10:5) She had heard a report about his words and wisdom back home (1 Kings 10:6), and seeing it was a whole different thing. I think even the burnt offerings at the house of the LORD stopped her in her tracks.

explanations.answer: She finds it a bit much
explanations.explanation: Nope, baker, she's not rolling her eyes at any of it. The text says it "…took her breath away." (1 Kings 10:5) She's amazed, not annoyed. Her next words are all praise (1 Kings 10:6-9).

That's a tough crowd, baker, but the queen isn't hunting for flaws. The text says seeing all this "…took her breath away." (1 Kings 10:5) She came with hard questions, and during her visit she says, "…not even half was told to me." (1 Kings 10:7) Nothing in the passage says she found anything lacking.

Not this time, baker. She says it herself: "…I did not believe these things until I came and saw with my own eyes." (1 Kings 10:7) She heard the report back home, but she needed to see it. Honestly, I respect a person who checks before she believes.

Right, baker. The queen of Sheba says, "But I did not believe these things until I came and saw with my own eyes." (1 Kings 10:7) She had heard the report in her own country, but seeing was what changed her mind. Honestly, I respect a person who checks before she believes.

Yes, baker. She says, "Indeed, not even half was told to me." (1 Kings 10:7) Then she adds, "Your wisdom and prosperity have far exceeded the report I heard." (1 Kings 10:7) Imagine a report so good that the real thing still beats it by miles.

Not quite, baker. She says the opposite: "Indeed, not even half was told to me." (1 Kings 10:7) The report was good, but what she saw went far past it. Her words are "…far exceeded the report I heard."

I get the thought, baker. But she says "…not even half was told to me." (1 Kings 10:7) She tells Solomon, "Your wisdom and prosperity have far exceeded the report I heard." (1 Kings 10:7) The real thing was bigger than the talk.

That's right, baker. The queen says, "Blessed be the LORD your God, who has delighted in you to set you on the throne of Israel." (1 Kings 10:9) She was praising the LORD, not just Solomon. She started out testing a king and ended up blessing his God.
Good thought, baker, since David was Solomon's father (1 Kings 2:12). But the queen never mentions him. She says, "Blessed be the LORD your God…" (1 Kings 10:9) Her blessing goes to the LORD.

Hiram does show up in this passage, baker, but not in her speech. Hiram, king of Tyre (1 Kings 5:1), has a fleet that brings gold and almug wood (1 Kings 10:11). The queen says, "Blessed be the LORD your God…" (1 Kings 10:9) Hiram's busy hauling cargo, so I'll let him off this one.

Yes, baker. The queen says the LORD "…has made you king to carry out justice and righteousness." (1 Kings 10:9) That's the purpose she names for the throne. I think that's a good thing to say with treasure piled up all around her.

Reasonable guess, baker, since kings and battles go together in people's minds. But the queen says the LORD "…has made you king to carry out justice and righteousness." (1 Kings 10:9) Armies aren't in her words. She names justice and righteousness.

That sounds like a king's dream, baker, but it isn't what she says. She says the LORD "…has made you king to carry out justice and righteousness." (1 Kings 10:9) Nothing about fear. Fame is in the passage, but the reason for the throne is justice and righteousness.

Yes, baker. The text says, "Never again were spices in such abundance brought in as those the queen of Sheba gave to King Solomon." (1 Kings 10:10) She also gave 120 talents of gold and precious stones. Spices like hers never came in again, and I can't even top my own last batch.

Not quite, baker. The text says, "Never again were spices in such abundance brought in as those the queen of Sheba gave to King Solomon." (1 Kings 10:10) So no spices brought in after hers matched that abundance.

That's it, baker. Solomon made the almug wood into steps for the house of the LORD and the palace, "…and into lyres and harps for the singers." (1 Kings 10:12) The text also says such almug wood had never been brought in before, and hasn't been seen again to this day. Rare wood, and some of it ended up making music.

Close, baker, since the house of the LORD is right there in the verse. But the text says the wood became "…lyres and harps for the singers." (1 Kings 10:12) The priests aren't mentioned in that sentence. The singers got the instruments.

I can picture it, baker, but it's not what the verse says. The almug wood became steps, and "…lyres and harps for the singers." (1 Kings 10:12) The singers are the ones named for the music-making gear.

That's right, baker. The text says, "So King Solomon surpassed all the kings of the earth in riches and wisdom." (1 Kings 10:23) Gold shields, an ivory throne and a stack of chariots all point that way. Solomon, king of Israel, was top of the list in both riches and wisdom.

Not this one, baker. The text says, "So King Solomon surpassed all the kings of the earth in riches and wisdom." (1 Kings 10:23) Both riches and wisdom, and all the kings of the earth. That's a pretty big crowd to beat.

explanations.answer: God put it in his heart
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. The text says the whole world sought Solomon "…to hear the wisdom that God had put in his heart." (1 Kings 10:24) The wisdom came from God. I think that's worth remembering whenever a person looks amazing.

explanations.answer: The queen of Sheba taught him
explanations.explanation: Fun idea, baker, but it runs the other way. She came to Solomon with her questions, and he answered them all (1 Kings 10:1-3). The text says his wisdom was what "…God had put in his heart." (1 Kings 10:24) She was the student in that room.

Egypt does come up in this passage, baker, but only for horses and chariots (1 Kings 10:28-29). The text never says Solomon studied there. It says people came to hear "…the wisdom that God had put in his heart." (1 Kings 10:24) The source of Solomon's wisdom was God.
